utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Unfortunately, Judge Van den Wyngaert is not able to sit today, and we expect she will sit possibly Tuesday of next week. She will be back and able to sit. We have decided to continue sitting under the rule. The affirmation that you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to all in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Korica.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones please be switched off, please, except for the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My name is Miroslav Vasic, I'm an attorney-at-law, and I have a few questions for you. Could you please pause after I finish putting my question. It worked yesterday with Mr. Lukic, so I hope that it will work today so that everyone in the courtroom can follow what we are saying and the interpreters can keep up with us. Thank you. First of all, yesterday, in response to Mr. Lukic's questions, you spoke about your military career and you said that you spent some time in the counter-intelligence group of the 1st Military District and from 1991, until 1993, Bogdan Vujic was your superior.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me properly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note they can hardly hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Bearing that in mind, I assume that you knew Mr. Vujic well and cooperated with him professionally; and there's one thing that struck me, what you said to the representatives of the OTP in The Hague. You said that Colonel Bogdan Vujic is prone to invent things; is that what you really said and is that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether, in your business cooperation, if I can put it that way, and if you say that his -- that he was your superior for a while, did you write reports together with Mr. Vujic and did he express that particular characteristic of his when he wrote official reports?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not in such a pronounced way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you just explain to us in a few sentences what this was all about, this tendency of his to twist things, to invent things?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think he invented things, but he would always add something, making his own effort more important.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So that his role would be enhanced in that way, did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: There's one thing that is unclear to me from your answers to Mr. Lukic's questions yesterday; it has to do with the name or nickname Colonel Branko. You explained that yesterday. You explained what happened, roughly, in Velepromet with Arkan and how come the colonel addressed Arkan as Colonel Branko. I'm not going to ask you about that again but as far as you know, at previous assignments and during this assignment in Vukovar, did he have a secret name as a security officer, as an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked for the security from 1959 until 1986, and never ever did I have a secret name, not in a single action, let alone bear a name like that all the time. None of my colleagues had a name like that either, and I never heard of Bogdan Vujic having a secret nickname, Colonel Branko.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we just go back for a moment to your answers from yesterday that had to do with contacts with Bogdan Vujic over the past few years, as you had put it, and his requests, if I can put it that way, that you come to his apartment to talk to him. I'm interested in the following: When you talked to him in his apartment, did he try to convince you that what he gave you as his statement that he gave to the OTP was, in actual fact, what did happen, although your view of things differed from that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I intervened on the spot, in his apartment, and I proved things to him and I showed things to him; for example, the IDs I had, I have them here with me. I showed him what weapons I had, and he added that to his statement, that I had a rifle. I never carried a rifle. And that is how I opposed some other things that he said by way of detail in his statement, on the spot, and as a matter of fact, I left demonstratively without having read it fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Korica. I'm not going to deal with Mr. Vujic's statement, but I will deal with the transcript, or rather, testimony before this Tribunal. I just want to ask you if he mentioned then that he invoked your name when he spoke of different events and did he ask you to confirm that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for what I read there, he didn't ask me to confirm anything that was not correct. I immediately said what I disagreed with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to the period you described here after your retirement, you came to your former unit, that's what you told us, and you said that actually by way of a joke, you were sent to combat action. Tell me, when you came to this unit, Major Muncan's unit, it was also a counter-intelligence unit like before, right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And it was under the command of the now late Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the professional control of Ljubisa Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said to us that the building where the headquarters or centre of this counter-intelligence group was was in the post office building in Sid, and you said that you worked on interviewing some persons who had been brought in and you said there were ethnic Croats and ethnic Serbs. Tell me, this centre where these persons were brought in, where was this centre where you interviewed people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That centre was I think in a place called Slovacki Dom, that is where people were brought in, and the military police were there. And a captain was in charge; I don't know whether he was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was this captain from the command of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know whether, in the building of the elementary school Sremski front in Sid there was a unit or a particular organ?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know -- well, I don't know what the name of the school is, but as far as I know, in Sid there weren't any other military security organs except for us, and the army was in one school; but I don't know whether they were ordinary soldiers or military policemen, but no security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know whether, in this area, there were any security organs of the air force and the air defence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not contact them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Vasic please switch off his microphone; we cannot hear the witness when the witness speaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us if you know or if you don't know who Zivanovic and Zaric are; do you know these persons?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, Mr. Korica, during your work in Sid, did you cooperate with a group that worked on interrogation and interviewing prisoners of war in Begeci?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any contact with them, and I didn't know who all the people working there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the words of Colonel Bogdan Vujic, he and his group were sent to the Vukovar front line by the security administration; did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what Captain Muncan had told us, that we were going there to reinforce the group from the security administration where Vujic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This group was sent by the security administration to carry out the triage and screening of members of the Croatian paramilitary forces, as you described yesterday, to separate them from the other civilians and, possibly within these groups, to find out who the war crimes suspects were?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you also said that the superior of your group was Bogdan Vujic; that's what he became at a certain point in time. Can you explain this to us, at what locations was he your superior, or rather, Captain Muncan, Major Muncan -- sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a captain then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Captain Muncan.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in view of the fact that Muncan explained that we were going to this group of the security administration and that there were three colonels there were, we were resubordinated to them. I was with Bogdan Vujic, and he was my superior in Velepromet and at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He was an officer from the superior command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you talked about how you came to Negoslavci and how, in the town command, you found these officers from the security administration where Colonel Mrksic, as commander of the command of Operations Group South - as is only proper when one comes to the territory of his unit - spoke to you and familiarised you with the situation in the territory and in his unit. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After that, you said that you went to Velepromet. I'm interested in two things only in respect of that: First of all, when you went that evening to Velepromet, on that day and on the following day, did you see Colonel Mrksic ever again at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see Colonel Mrksic at all after that, throughout my stay in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question: You said that you went to Velepromet in cars. Can we be more specific. How did you travel and how did this group from the security administration travel? I mean, I'm not talking about types of vehicles, but did you go on foot or by car?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all went by car, two cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind to tell us how it was that you returned from Velepromet and Negoslavci around 1.00 that night, as you told us?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned with Captain Muncan in my group by car, the same car that took me there. I don't know how Bogdan Vujic came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you telling us that you didn't see how he came back?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see how he came back. I did not see how Kijanovic and Tomic came back either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you told us about how you came to Velepromet on the 19th of November and, as you said, it was under the control of the Territorial Defence. Could you now please tell me who took over control over the evacuation of these persons from Velepromet when this group from the security administration arrived and when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Bogdan Vujic who took over control. Tomic and Kijanovic never issued any orders to me. Vujic contacted Ljubinko as well, Ljubinko Stojanovic, and Captain Borisavljevic, and all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he issue any orders regarding activities that should be taken by way of preparing the transport of these persons, the compiling of lists? Was that done on orders from Bogdan Vujic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lists were made on orders from Bogdan Vujic, namely when the buses arrived -- there weren't any preparations regarding this, but when the buses arrived, he said that these people would be taken out of the hangar and boarded on to these buses. How they should sit down, or rather, how they should board the buses, that all the seats should be taken, and that all should have proper seats, that no one should be allowed to stand in the bus. And in every bus, there should be one officer who would write down the names of all the persons who were on the bus and then to hand these lists over to Srecko Borisavljevic, which is exactly what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, knowing Bogdan Vujic, would he have been likely to take all necessary steps, including the use of force or weapons, had there been any attempts to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The witness is being asked for his opinion on the matter. It's my submission that that is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, your question seems to be searching for an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question begins by asking for an opinion, but I'm afraid my learned friend did not allow me to complete my question. What I'm trying to ask the witness - since the witness was physically present at Velepromet as was Mr. Vujic - is to tell me about some of the events described by Mr. Vujic in his evidence. We have a witness here who is exceptionally familiar with Mr. Vujic and familiar with his reactions in a professional context. This is what I was about to ask him: Had those people at Velepromet, being attacked, harassed or even killed, would Bogdan Vujic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can't ask for an opinion like that. You can ask what he saw Vujic do; what situations arose while he was there, if you need to; but going for an opinion as to what he thinks Vujic would have done if some situation arose is not the way we can allow the evidence to run. It's opinion on conjecture.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Korica, while you were at Velepromet, did you see anyone kill any persons there, beat them, or indeed harass them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I saw no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You spent most of your time at Velepromet with Bogdan Vujic, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 90 per cent of the time I spent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: According to the rules of service, what would a security officer be expected to do or be required to do if anyone were to attack any persons that he was in charge of securing and evacuating?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That officer would have had to enlist the assistance of the military police in order to foil any such threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would he have been authorised to order the use of weapons?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would he not have been required, once the situation had been dealt with and back to normal, to arrest those persons who were being violent and perhaps take steps against them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Bogdan Vujic at Velepromet on the 19th of November telling anyone things like: Get back to your senses, Vojvodo. Was there anything like that happening?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when those persons were getting on to the buses, the military police had arrived. They were securing the buses, and there was this man called Topola who was not able to get on to a bus with Bogdan Vujic compiling lists. There was something like that being uttered, but I didn't quite catch the whole sentence. Later on, however, Vujic and the other people who were there, quoted the sentence to me in that form.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you at the time whether Topola actually physically clashed with Vujic or was he just standing there at the door of the bus?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of any physical contact or clash between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Had anyone attacked an officer, a security officer in this case, in the line of duty what would that security officer have been authorised to do about that? What would he have been supposed to do under the rules of service that applied at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me a hypothetical question. I'm telling you nothing much happened. It's very difficult to answer what he would have done, given the set of circumstances you described.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I am not asking you what he would have done, I'm asking you about the law. What would an officer like that be authorised to do if attacked in the line of duty? Would he have the right to defend himself, to use a firearm, or even kill that person in order to protect himself? Is this not something that is clearly defined in the rules of service?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that is clearly envisaged in relation to all persons, civilians included. Everyone has the right to protect himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, 1991, while at Velepromet, did you hear Bogdan Vujic order anyone to use force or weapons?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing like that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now be putting to you sections of Mr. Vujic's evidence, specifically in relation to him saying that you specifically did certain things. So this is what I'd like to ask you. I would like to ask you if the things that he said of you were true.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is dated the 16th of November, for the Court's reference and my learned friend's reference. 4510 is the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: He says that at one point at Velepromet, you came up to him and told him that certain persons like Marko Crevar and Topola were saying that they wanted to kill him along with the Ustashas. Is this something you told him at Velepromet on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The 16th -- rather, the transcript reference is 4520, Bogdan Vujic's evidence on the 17th of February, 2006. Mr. Vujic claims that you told him, once the evacuation had started of persons on to those buses, that some TO men, Chetniks specifically, were taking people away from Velepromet and that those people were not seen again and that there were bursts of gun-fire being heard nearby. You said this was the doing of Marko Crevar, who had previously said that he would kill him too along with the Ustashas. Is this true? Is this something you told Bogdan Vujic on the 19th of November at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a complete fabrication. They did react, but Crevar talked to me. It was a perfectly normal conversation. It wasn't always Crevar, but those people were tipsy and their reaction was: Why were we protecting those people? But did I say that they were taking people away? Did I see them taking people away? I would have been the first to stop it, and I most certainly would have informed Colonel Vujic and Borisavljevic as well to try to get them to stop it. However, I never said that, I never saw that, I never heard that, nor indeed, did I ever hear any bursts of gun-fire behind the hangar. As for behind the hangar and the villages and the surroundings, well, everyone saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You explained that in answer to a question by my learned friend, Mr. Lukic, yesterday. Thank you. You say that you returned to Negoslavci sometime past 1.00 at night. You say that you went straight to the operations room at the command post of OG South, you spent the night there. You say that Colonel Mrksic was no longer around when you arrived, only the duty officer was there. Was my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed it was, but I'm not quite positive. I do have a belief that the only person still around was the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said yesterday that Colonel Vujic arrived after you and he stayed with you through that night until the following morning. Did I get that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The next day, you say you were off to the hospital. What time did you arrive there, if you can remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was sometime at around 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us what you did there. You said it took just over two hours. Do you remember when you eventually left the hospital and came back to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we left the hospital at about 10.00, and we soon made it back to Velepromet. We drove there in the military vehicle en route for Negoslavci, and they still had room enough inside the vehicle to take us along. I'm not sure how long it took, but we didn't stop anywhere on the way. Sometime past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What would you say, sir, if I told you that there is a person claiming that they came with you to Velepromet and that they arrived after 12.00? This is one of the security officers from the security administration saying that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not drive with any such person then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who did you drive with in that vehicle that you mentioned on your way to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Bogdan Vujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived at Velepromet with Bogdan Vujic, you say you spent some time in an office which you believe was Ljubinko Stojanovic's office. Did I get that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At first I thought it was Borisavljevic's office, but I later found out that this was Ljubinko's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you told us about what happened in Ljubinko Stojanovic's office while you were there. You also talked about Bogdan Vujic's departure to attend that cabinet meeting. I want to know something about something that happened after the cabinet meeting. Bogdan Vujic told you about the meeting. When he returned, did he tell you that he was afraid for his life and that he had been a sort of hostage at that meeting, at that cabinet meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogdan Vujic said no such thing at the time. He did -- at a later stage, he told me about that, but what he told me at the time was a short but honest account, or at least that's what I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We will return to that later on. Once he had told you about what had happened at the cabinet meeting, did Bogdan Vujic go out into Velepromet's yard before he was off to barracks on that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the room at one point; Bogdan Vujic remained inside. This was when I saw Goran Hadzic, who was the only person I recognised. I do not know anybody else. We exchanged greetings, but at this point in time Bogdan Vujic did not leave the room. He did go outside later on. He went outside into the yard. I don't know what he did, because I wasn't with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this: Do you remember Bogdan Vujic leaving, going outside before the cabinet meeting? What would you say, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he ever left or went outside before the cabinet meeting. I can't be positive, but I think he sat down to write some notes and I was fiddling with that handbag. But I don't think he ever left the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How much time elapsed between the time you left Velepromet and the time Bogdan Vujic sat down to write those notes and before he was eventually called to that cabinet meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over an hour, I'm certain about that. Perhaps even as many as two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Bogdan Vujic claims that the cabinet meeting began past 1300 hours; would that jog your memory, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That changes nothing, I think. I don't know when exactly we arrived, but -- from the hospital. I'm not certain if it was 10.00 or possibly half past 10.00. It changes nothing about my perception of the time-line or how long we stayed inside to do some work. It changes nothing. It is certainly possible that the meeting began at 1300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind, sir, as to repeat what it was exactly that Bogdan Vujic told you once he was back from the cabinet meeting, what you told us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, he told me that he had quarrelled with the people there because they had asked him to surrender the prisoners to them, saying that the prisoners belonged to them. So that is what the main quarrel was about. He said Arkan was the only armed person there, but he did not take part in the cabinet's work. He told me there was a severe exchange between him, on the one hand, and the cabinet members, on the other, about the exchange of prisoners. He made a threat at one time that he would get a cameraman there to record the proceedings and then the -- what the prime minister, Goran Hadzic, said that they would attack them with tanks -- that they would attack JNA tanks if they had been -- if they were allowed to take the prisoners away.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he say anything else that was of any importance at all or was this how the cabinet meeting ended?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know whether he said anything else that was important or not. I can't remember right now. He may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he perhaps mention that he had been attacked there, or that he had told them that he was there on behalf of the Supreme Command and the chief of the security administration?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he say that he had told them that there would be no question of surrendering those prisoners because they would have to be sent to Sremska Mitrovica, being JNA prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't say things like that to me. If indeed he had been there on behalf of the Supreme Command, then he might as well have surrendered those prisoners. It's certainly not something he shared with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he perhaps tell you if this cabinet meeting was attended by any other officers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. You see, it slipped my mind a moment ago. He told me that halfway through the meeting in mid-stream, as it were, as they were busy debating, a colonel arrived. He wasn't sure which unit this colonel belonged to, whether he was a member of the Guards Brigade or whether he had arrived from Belgrade. He brought some sort of a document and told them that if that was the decision eventually taken, in that case, they could set up a POW camp, which is what they had been asking for, clamouring for.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember his exact words, how he told you this? Is what you told us a moment ago an accurate reflection of his words at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say 99 per cent perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that Mr. Vujic could not have said any such thing to you because he himself had not heard what the lieutenant-colonel said at this government session, would that change your view?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reference is pages 4562 and 4563 for the Court and my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that another witness also did not mention that no approval for setting up a POW camp was referred to, would that jog your memory or change your view?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't change anything, because Bogdan Vujic told me that immediately after that there was rejoicing in that office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm late, but I'm objecting now because the witness is talking about indirect knowledge, what Bogdan Vujic told him. Now would what third persons said change his view in terms of the indirect knowledge he had? It's not that he has any direct knowledge. He's just sharing with us what Vujic shared with him, so that's why I think this is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm -- I haven't grasped your point, I'm afraid, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems I'm too complicated. I am not challenging Mr. Vasic's right to ask the witness what Vujic said to him, but then he puts the statement of another witness to this witness, asking him whether that witness's statement would change his view in terms of what Vujic had said to him. That is why I believe we're entering the field of speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm getting some glimpses of what you're concerned about, Mr. Lukic, but I think at the moment, it's premature. If it develops much further, we will have to intervene. But for the moment, carry on, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm about to finish this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As for your conversation with Mr. Vujic, did you inform Mr. Muncan or Colonel Petkovic about it the same day, straight away?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed Muncan -- now, whether Muncan informed Petkovic, I don't know, but immediately upon arriving in Sid, he went to Petkovic's for a briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you find out whether he briefed Petkovic about this information that you had, namely that some government was establishing some POW camp, as you had put it, in the zone of responsibility of the 1st Military District? Did Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not control my superior as to what it was he said during a briefing. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you inform your superior in writing or orally?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orally. Only when I have a direct conversation, then I compile a note on that conversation or interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The security of the 1st Military District, wouldn't it have to be aware of this kind of fact, that on its territory the government of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Zapadni Srem is about to set up some POW camp, wouldn't they have to know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I was not in charge and that was not my line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in November 1991, General Vlado Stojanovic issued an order that no POW exchange can be carried out without his approval? Were you familiarised with that order of the command of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of work you are referring to because I think that interviews were never prohibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Obviously you didn't hear me well. I asked about exchanges. I wasn't asking about work. Did you see an order issued by the command of the 1st Military District prohibiting any POW exchanges without the approval of General Vlado Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this order. It was sufficient for me to have my superiors see that because I did not engage in such exchanges of POWs anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that later, when many left Velepromet, that Vujic went to the barracks and you, with Muncan and others from the group, went to Ovcara. Did I understand you right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understood me right. Vujic left a bit earlier. I stayed on at Velepromet to wait for Muncan. He came -- well, pretty late, just before it got dark. He came to pick me up, and from there we went straight to Sid but we stopped by at Ovcara as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, when you went in the direction of Ovcara, did you ask someone where this was, did you know? How did you find this particular locality?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you please go on.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Muncan knew or somebody in Velepromet told him that there is this road that goes to the left when you pass the barracks. There is this road that goes straight to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Since you have mentioned Muncan now, did he tell you why they were in barracks on that day? What were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, except for me and Vujic, both of these groups went to Velepromet to help out there because there were still quite a few people there and -- namely men, women, and children. When they finished that and we came to Velepromet, we didn't find them there; they just told us that they went to the barracks, but I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't say that you were there, but did they tell you why it was that they went to the barracks; what kind of business did they have in the barracks, this group of yours; and were there any officers there from the security administration group?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard - Muncan told me about this later in the car - that they all went there because they had been informed that the buses were there and that there were some incidents caused by territorials, that they were attacking these prisoners who were on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us that these incidents were resolved, that the buses were secured. Did they tell you how long the officers were at the barracks, and were they there after the buses were secured and after these incidents were resolved?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't tell me about these details. I know that they stayed there, and they told me that the buses were secured and they went in the direction of Ovcara. And then they thought that they had no further work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After the buses went to Ovcara, did they stay on in the barracks or did they leave the barracks then? Did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. They did not tell me exactly how much time they spent where. I really have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you when the buses left the barracks for Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't tell me that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And did they tell you why the buses went to Ovcara from the barracks?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear of that reason either. We really weren't up to talking. We hadn't slept for two days and, to tell you the truth, he didn't tell me why they went to Ovcara; but he said we would stop by there to see whether the conditions were right for any kind of interviews for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Before you went to Ovcara, did Mr. Muncan tell you whether the group had been at Ovcara on that day? Had they gone there straight from the barracks?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand you. What group?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sorry, maybe I'm not very clear. The group of officers including Mr. Muncan and these other officers from the security administration. If you know, did Mr. Muncan tell you whether they went from the barracks to Ovcara before they came to you in Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think that Muncan first came when we came there together by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And do you know about the officers from the security administration?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I did not see Vujic afterwards or the officers from the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you went to Ovcara that day at dusk, why your group went there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muncan told us to go there to -- that we were going there to see what the situation was like and whether we could have a few interviews with some individuals from that group, and that was the only reason why we went to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That is one of the basic tasks involved in these interviews, to see the status of persons who are possible perpetrators of criminal offences; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you came to Ovcara, you said it was dark or dusk, rather. You told us that you stayed in the car together with Mr. Radakovic; did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Then, near the hangar, did you see a white Renault 4 and some JNA officer in it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no such vehicle there, that vehicle or any other vehicle like ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know then that the prisoners were being guarded by the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had a pass for moving about throughout the territory, and this was under the control of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just a small digression. When you came to Vukovar, did you hear about the surrender of the Mitnica group on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard something about that, but I don't know about the details. I heard that these people were evacuated to Sremska Mitrovica; that's the only thing I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were these people interviewed by persons from the security of the 1st Military District; do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our group was not involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these persons were at Ovcara between the 18th and the 19th and that they were also guarded by the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What did Mr. Muncan tell you when he returned, and how long did he stay at the hangar?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that he stayed there for five or six minutes, then he came back and he sort of waved his hand and said: There are no conditions here for any interviews. It's getting dark. There is no separate room anywhere. Let's go home to Sid. And there is time for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us what that means, "And there is time for that." Does that mean that interviews with these persons would be conducted some other time or what?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you who he had talked to, who received him in the hangar, whether he introduced himself to someone? Did he mention any such thing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say a word about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he say who was in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that the prisoners were in the hangar and that they were standing or sitting by the walls throughout the hangar. That's the only thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he say that these persons were guarded, that they had some guards guarding them there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw policemen in front, but I don't know whether there was anybody inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether they told him that these people would stay on there for a triage to be carried out or that they would be sent somewhere? Did Mr. Muncan, your superior, tell you any such thing at that moment?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muncan did not tell us anything else about these men or that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was your direct superior, Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic, informed about this situation that same day when you arrived in Sid?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muncan told us when he returned from the briefing that he had informed Colonel Petkovic about everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he share any details of that briefing with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Colonel Bogdan Vujic, on the 21st of November, 1991, went to see Colonel Petkovic with some sort of a presentation or did he submit a report, or indeed anyone from Bogdan Vujic's group? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you testified that up until March 1992 you had been in Vukovar and had heard nothing about what had occurred at Ovcara. Your task was to investigate crimes, to gather documents on any crimes, and to conduct interviews. In your work, did you ever come across the town commander Lieutenant-Colonel Milorad Vojinovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really have such a good head for names, but yes, I was once at the town command, as they called it. Truth to tell, I can't remember the reason for my being there, but the answer is I must have seen the lieutenant-colonel, if indeed that was the person who was the town commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Korica, bearing in mind what my learned friend Mr. Lukic said yesterday, do you perhaps want to have a break now? I am nearing the end of my cross-examination. I am nearly there, but in view of your health, I don't know what your choice would be.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I feel now, I think we can press ahead and have our break at the usual time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, I would like to press on, since I am close to the end. In your work, did you have any contacts with the chief of security of the 80th Motorised Brigade at the Vukovar town command, Dragi Vukosavljevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe two or three times, especially later on. We knew each other quite well. I think he originally hailed from Kragujevacka Raca.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That's quite correct. Throughout that time did you entertain any contacts with Captain Vezmarovic, the commander of the military police company of the 80th Motorised Brigade, who was also in charge of town security in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I may have seen him or talked to him but nothing special that I'd remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Korica, did any of these persons ever tell you about what had happened at Ovcara? I'm talking before March 1992, which is as long as you were in the area. You were studying evidence and gathering evidence about crimes that had occurred in that area, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever told me anything about Ovcara. All we knew, or at least what we were told, was that those people had been sent away to Sremska Mitrovica and that was where our responsibilities stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Korica, who was in charge of the Sremska Mitrovica prison or, rather, this provisional POW camp that was set up where security officers conducted interviews?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see an order by the security administration appointing security officers from the 1st Military District to conduct interviews at this camp together with officers from the security administration? Did you ever find out that Mr. Bogdan Vujic was, in fact, one of the interrogators at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that, but your question was did I ever see an order. The answer is no, I never saw an order, but I did see the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did those people know that the POWs had been transported to Sremska Mitrovica or indeed that they had ever got there, arrived in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, nor did I ask them. I drove one person to Sremska Mitrovica one night. I surrendered him to Vujic, as well as the bag. And that was as much as I knew about the people. But I did know the people who worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did your group, including Mr. Muncan, ever receive an assignment from Mr. Ljubisa Petkovic to conduct an interview or submit a report in relation to the group that you had toured at Ovcara the evening of the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Korica. I have no further questions for you. Your Honours, this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Korica.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You know that one of the accused in this case is the then-Captain Miroslav Radic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav who?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Radic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 20th of November, 1991, you said there was a triage; those captured at the hospital were being separated off or selected. You gave a detailed account of which officers were involved in that. Therefore, my first question: Throughout that process of selecting prisoners and in the sense of ordering anything or assisting, was Miroslav Radic, Captain Miroslav Radic, involved in this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember ever seeing Miroslav Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean he wasn't involved in the so-called selection process at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my last question, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We could break now, Mr. Moore, or we could, it seems, go on for about a quarter of an hour. What would be most convenient?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm quite happy to continue for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Korica, we meet again.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you one or two little matters before we break. Simply this: Clearly, I have listened to your evidence, and if one looks at your evidence from the time you arrive in the Vukovar area until, let us say, the 21st of November, so we're talking evening of the 19th, day of the 20th, indeed we can leave it there, would it be right to say that the only aggression or unpleasant act that you ever saw was from one person and that was from a gentleman called Topola, and that everything else was normal? Would that be a fair general summary of what you saw?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for aggression, I think that might just be right; but nothing there was pleasant or indeed normal, so much for that. As for aggressive behaviour, or aggression, there were no acts of aggression, apart from those committed by Topola.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you would agree with me, the only thing you ever saw was Topola being aggressive. You saw nothing else that constituted aggression?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the Velepromet facility on the evening of the 19th?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on the 19th, I must have spent at least three hours at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And forgive me, it is my memory that fails with advancing years, if one is talking about the time that you got there and the time you left, what time are we talking about that you were at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we arrived at Velepromet at about half past 10.00 and were back past 1.00, past midnight, back to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The sound of typing interferes with the witness's voice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When we are talking about the Velepromet facility, it is not a particularly big facility, is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Velepromet was a wholesale agency or company. It was a large area with agricultural machinery and that sort of thing. The building itself is rather small. There were a number of hangars there, but I didn't go there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if one was talking about your brief or the task that you had when you went to Velepromet, how would you describe your understanding of the task at Velepromet that you were required to do?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we were required to do was to help with evacuating those who had arrived from the hospital as well as from elsewhere. The TO men were bringing people in one-by-one. We were to help those people being evacuated because they said the buses for their evacuation would soon be there. They said we should go and speak to Stojanovic and to Captain Borisavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if one looks at this in the round, would it be right to say that your brief, your task, was to see how the situation was, because apparently it was rather difficult and complicated; find out if you could assist; and then report back to let everybody know what could or could not be achieved. Would that be a fair way of assessing it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll come back to Velepromet later on. I just want to inquire about one other aspect of your evidence before the break. Do you remember you told us that you were -- you had a briefing with Major Sljivancanin when you first arrived at Negoslavci; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that. I never said that we briefed Sljivancanin anywhere at any time, nor did we. It was Sljivancanin who told us what we were supposed to do on that particular day as well as the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps there's just a slight error in the translation. What I'm talking about is a briefing from Sljivancanin to you on the evening of the 19th at Negoslavci. Do you remember that? That is what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not trying to catch you out, Mr. Korica; I'm just trying to clarify one or two matters. In your evidence yesterday, you said the following: "Sljivancanin told us that the main task for us for the following day, and that we would be conducting screening in the hospital and that we would send some people to Sremska Mitrovica. He said that it was because there were many people there who had taken shelter in the hospital and didn't go to the Velepromet compound when they were told that they could go there. He said that there were some members of the ZNG, of the MUP, and that there were war criminals who had taken shelter in the hospital and camouflaged themselves in doctors' uniforms." Now, that was what you said yesterday. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it went on, and this is at line 14726, or page 14726, line 18: "He said that those people needed to be separated and that everything needed to be cleared at the hospital and prepared for the arrival of the International Red Cross, so as to avoid any incident." Now, I want to just deal with that last part because, again, these are your words; I'm just reading them back. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that when he said, "These people needed to be separated," that he was referring to the ZNG, MUP, and the criminals who had taken shelter in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was all those who weren't hospital staff had to be separated off; therefore, this included the MUP and ZNG there, that much is certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I want to read back exactly your words: "He said that there were some members of the ZNG, of the MUP, and that there were war criminals who had taken shelter in the hospital and camouflaged themselves in doctors' uniforms. He said that those people needed to be separated and that everything needed to be cleared at the hospital and prepared for the arrival of the International Red Cross." So what I'm suggesting to you, when you look at your evidence and what Mr. Sljivancanin has said to you, when he refers to "those people," it's the ZNG, the MUP, and the criminals who had taken shelter in the hospital and had used doctors' clothing to camouflage themselves. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. However, at the time, we had no time to ask who was ZNG and who was MUP or whatever. This included those who weren't hospital staff, who were not patients, and were not wounded. We just separated them off and left the final triage for Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now what I want to ask you is this: The phrase that "they need to be separated," we've dealt with that, and that "everything needed to be cleared at the hospital and prepared for the arrival of the ICRC so as to avoid any incident." Now, those are your words; they're not anything that I'm making up. Can we take it that what you meant was that that selection process, that triage was to be done before the arrival of the ICRC, so to avoid any incident with them? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only with them, but also about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can we deal with the two words. I'll deal with "with them." So they had to be gone before them -- could you please not look at Mr. Lukic. Can you just try and look at me for a moment. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. Obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's all right. So the intention was that those people were to be selected before the ICRC arrived, yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so that was to avoid any incident, incident between the ICRC and, I don't know, perhaps the JNA.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably wasn't just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, then, so as to "avoid any incident." What do you mean by "avoid any incident"? Doesn't that refer to the fact that the ICRC were coming?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew the ICRC were coming, and nobody could have stopped them; however, there were some extremists there as well as armed people, all sorts of things. You had to have a look when the triage was being conducted to see whether any weapons were concealed in the area, because that is, after all, how we found the grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just finish with this final question before the break. There are ZNGs, Mr. Sljivancanin would say, there is the MUP, there are the criminals; how can you select them without some points of reference? How were you to choose those people? How were you to isolate those people; can you tell me, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, Sljivancanin did not share these specifics with us. The important thing was to separate off all persons who weren't medical staff or hospital staff. For example, if someone was a hospital driver, they would have had some sort of a document to show for that. The hospital staff were the only ones allowed to stay at the hospital as well as the wounded with whom we had no contact at all, because it was the military doctors who were in charge of that, who, as far as I heard, at the time, had arrived from Novi Sad. As for everything else, all those other people remaining who were outside those two boxes or categories included the MUP, the criminals, those who perpetrated crimes and evil-doers, but their triage was to take place at Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I said "the last question"; it's always fatal for a barrister to say last question. If they were going to Sremska Mitrovica, isn't it normal to take a list of people who you collect so that when you are transporting them and at hand-over, you have a list of names for people going out and that same list to take them off at the other end. That's right, I think, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe that's what we should have done, but the order we received was to write things down. Maybe there was somebody else at a different stage when those persons were being searched or placed on the buses, maybe somebody should have written things down there, but this is not something that I know anything at all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. We'll resume, with His Honour's leave, at an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a 20-minute break now and resume at ten past 4.00. The court officer will help you out, Mr. Korica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Korica, may I just deal with the start of your evidence, and I'll try and deal with it sequentially, A followed by B. You've told us that when the group was created, for example, there was Tomic, Stosic, Kijanovic, yourself and others, I think -- did you travel by two cars to Sid?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I travelled with Muncan, and that group of ours that came before them came only for this situation; and I was in this group of Muncan's before. They did not go with us. They took their own car. And, as far as I heard later, they stopped by in Negoslavci. We didn't stop by anywhere. We went directly to Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I know this is a dreadful generalisation, but might it be right to say that sometimes when you're dealing with officers, they don't always tell you what's going on; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the case in our service. We all do our own job and we don't meddle with anybody else's jobs. As for the normal relationship between a senior officers and NCOs, there was no such distinction. We did know a lot of things that they were supposed to know but we weren't, we still knew a lot of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We call that in English the "grape-vine." You tended to know unofficially what was happening; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could you just say yes so it goes on the record? You nodded your head, you see.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't really understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. With your group, you tended to exchange information; would that be a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the exchange of information, is one of the reasons why you exchanged such information because it helps other members of that group understand what the problems or difficulties might be?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we would report to our superior, except in certain cases; but usually, we all reported together. We would be in the same room and we would submit reports as to what we did on that day, so that others would know what each and every one of us did within that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if there were difficulties for one member of the group, they would tend to tell the other members to help them understand the problems; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it can be put that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with Sid for a moment. Can I suggest that the instructions that were given by Babic at that time was that your group were not to take over any command responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not even know that Babic was in Sid, and I don't know what kind of instructions he gave. Otherwise, we did not have any kind of command of that sort -- command responsibility, that is, in our service even before that and not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can we just agree -- as I say, I'm not trying to catch you out in any way at all. Wherever it came from, there was a view that one should not take over any command responsibility; would that be a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, since we did not have any command responsibility. We did not have any command powers and, therefore, we did not have any command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could other microphones please be switched off while the witness is speaking the interpreters note. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to disturb this line of questioning, but I think that when the Prosecutor asked about what Babic had said, when he mentioned Sid, I don't know whether it was clear to the witness because when the witness spoke during the first part, the only time he mentioned Babic was in Belgrade. If that's what the Prosecutor wanted to clarify so that there wouldn't be any confusion, as Mr. Moore said himself, maybe it would be good if he said what conversation he meant between Colonel Babic and the witness, just to have things perfectly clear. That is what I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can move on in relation to this. So the witness has said that they didn't have any command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you understand that your task was to separate groups as opposed to not performing a triage?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my understanding was that this was a general triage or an initial triage, not a detailed triage because there weren't the right conditions for that and there wasn't enough time either. Not only separation, because separation had already been carried out. The doctors were on one side and the hospital staff. Others went -- had already gone out because they were told that they could go to Velepromet straight away. As for the remaining people there, those who were camouflaged as the sick or the wounded or who were introducing themselves in different ways so as to be able to leave with the convoy, well that is what we were supposed to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But what I'm trying to get at is before you actually get to Negoslavci, that in actual fact, there was a belief that the task was to separate, very generally, not to perform - your words - a specific triage. Would that be right? Would that be a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be put that way because Mr. Sljivancanin told us that Vesna Bosanac would help us in that, who was supposed to make a list of the hospital staff. Since that had not been done, then we were supposed to do that, or rather, this was done by the doctors and Mr. Sljivancanin. I think that Vesna Bosanac was there as well. Then after that separation, we carried out a triage of the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with the meeting with Mr. Mrksic. I just want to deal with that topic now. You told us that Mr. Mrksic spoke for approximately half an hour; you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And he was indicating to you in general terms, the military situation and situation that existed at that time within his zone of responsibility; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you remember an incident occurring through that briefing when, I believe, a young officer came in and explained to Colonel Mrksic that, I think, there had been three young soldiers killed recently; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you just remind us exactly what you remember occurring on that matter?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the duty officer who entered or the operations officer who was on duty. He came to Colonel Mrksic and said, Colonel, one of our vehicles hit a mine and three soldiers got killed. Mr. Mrksic replied to him, Put that in the graph and later on we will talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that Mr. Mrksic, in very general terms, indicated what was required at Velepromet and the hospital, but the person who was going to deal with it specifically was Mr. Sljivancanin, and that's why you had to wait for him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic told us about the general situation and about the situation in his zone of responsibility and in his unit, and the problems, and how many wounded there were, and how many persons were killed. It was a high number. As for the hospital and Velepromet, he said some things in general terms, that some people had already left the hospital and had gone to Velepromet. But with regard to all of this work, Mr. Sljivancanin would tell us about that in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know why Mr. Sljivancanin was telling you that information in detail?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because we came there to do that, so that we would familiarise ourselves with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Maybe it's the way I phrased the question, but why was it necessary -- or why was Mr. Sljivancanin telling you the details? What role was he playing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we knew that Mr. Sljivancanin was the security organ of the brigade and, for the most part, these were police and security tasks that we were supposed to carry out in the hospital and in Velepromet, so that is why we all came there, as a reinforcement, to help him carry out these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, trying to be fair about it, would it be right to say that your understanding was that Mr. Mrksic had delegated the responsibility for the evacuation to Mr. Sljivancanin, and that's why he was explaining in detail?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what they had agreed upon. It is only natural that this should be done by the security and the police and everyone knows who they are subordinated to. Both the security and police are subordinated to the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Lukic wanted to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The moment's passed, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you just explain to me what you mean by: "This is the sort of work that the security organ would do normally." Can you explain that to me in a little more detail for my understanding?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically it's not only the security organ that was working there. We came to help him. As for that part of the work in the hospital then, it was practically Colonel Vujic who was in charge. He was the ranking officer. But in terms of the professional line of work and his familiarity with the situation, it was only natural for Mr. Sljivancanin to do the work that he did with the doctors from Novi Sad, too. So the physicians were involved in that. The police were providing security outside, the police were carrying out searches, and it was the security organ who was in charge of the police, according to the professional line of work, and the commander was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What happens when a commander delegates his authority to a person? Does that person then take over the responsibilities of the commander? Can you just explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have such an opportunity, but perhaps it would be natural for him to take over the responsibilities as well if the authority to command had been transferred or delegated. It is one thing to work along the professional line, and it's a different thing to command. I don't know whether Mr. Sljivancanin commanded this entire operation or not, and I don't know what authority was transferred to him or delegated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I take you on in time to the trip in the vehicle from Negoslavci to the hospital. Can I just focus on that period. Mr. Sljivancanin was in the vehicle with you then; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you told us that he had informed you, as a group, what the tasks were to be; you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you just expand that. Can you just tell us what you mean by that. When you talk about tasks, what are you referring to? Forgive me, I don't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he said what the basic task was that we were supposed to carry out. He explained some things in greater detail while in the vehicle, who would do what. So he told us that there would be quite a bit of work because there would be very little assistance coming from Vesna Bosanac as the director of the hospital, so that we would have some difficulty. He would have a meeting with them, and make it possible for the hospital staff to be separated from others who are not hospital staff and who are not wounded; they would go to the other side. And once that is done, then we would come in. We would take people outside, those who had stayed behind and do not belong to this remaining group of hospital staff and the wounded. Then we took all such persons out. That is what he briefly explained to us in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You used the phrase: "We would come in." Who's the "we"? Is that yourself and Bogdan Vujic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's me and Bogdan Vujic -- well, it's not that I think. That is the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So how did Mr. Vujic react to being told what he had to be -- do by a major? Did he accept what was being said?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fully. It wasn't some order, it was sort of -- well, the man who knew the situation in the hospital the best. It was only natural for him to say how it would best be done. It doesn't have to be in the form of an order; it can be in the form of a proposal, how something can be done successfully. So I did not see any reaction on Bogdan Vujic's part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So it's not an order, but it's a proposal that has the same effect?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The effect is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I then go back in time to you coming to Mrksic, he giving you the general material, and then Mr. Sljivancanin coming, I think about half an hour. I'm sorry for taking you out of sequence, but I had to do it for really continuity. When Mr. Mrksic said to you for you to sit there and wait for Sljivancanin about the tasks, what did you understand by the phrase "tasks" that were to be done?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
