utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether the word was "zaduzenja," as in tasks, but we waited for Sljivancanin to inform us in greater detail about what it was that we were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to move on. I'm going to leave that area for the moment - I may come back - but I want to move on to the arrival at Velepromet itself, all right? So you went there by car. And forgive me, it is my memory, I think you said you were there from about 10.00 until 1.00. If I got that wrong, that's my fault, not yours. But was Borisavljevic expecting you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I don't know specifically, because Bogdan Vujic arrived earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin clearly had mentioned Velepromet. I don't know if you are aware - and there is no dispute about the matter - but Borisavljevic is subordinated to Sljivancanin, he's a member of the security organ; did you know that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. That evening, I didn't know that it was the security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Borisavljevic is a member of the security organ -- or was a member of the security organ at the time you went to Velepromet. There won't be any dispute about that. So you weren't aware that the security organ were there at that time. You thought he was just a JNA officer; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does it surprise you that Mr. Borisavljevic is a member of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I'm not surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you have been surprised that night, however?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe I wouldn't have. In that big commotion, it's very hard to find one's way. He wanted to be everywhere, to help out everywhere. Wherever somebody would be hurt, he would be there. So it wasn't easy to conclude anything different about him rather than -- that he made an effort to do good things there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us that Borisavljevic and Vujic had had a discussion. Did you see Tomic and Kijanovic at Velepromet at the start?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the start, I did. I saw the entire group. But I didn't know at the start who was Tomic, who was Vujanovic [as interpreted], and who was this fourth person. And when I came, they had already been at this meeting where I had not been. That meeting was attended by Ljubinko Stojanovic, at that office there, because he needed some vehicle, whatever, he went to that office; and that meeting was over quickly and they went out. That's when I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you were aware of Tomic and you were aware, perhaps later, I don't know, of Kijanovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew because they were at Mr. Mrksic's; we were all there together at Mr. Mrksic's. I know them from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As far as you could see, they were also going around Velepromet attempting to assist and assess the situation; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know something, you know what the situation was like over there, what one could see what was happening in that clearing at Velepromet outside those buildings, it's quite a large area, in fact. By night, there was no light there, so someone going behind the hangar and walking around Velepromet would have been sheer madness. Night-time is night-time, and the war was never over for us -- day-time is day-time, sure thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So therefore, anybody walking around in night-time, was not always easy to see; is that really what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that too, but I'm also saying that even we didn't dare go there, into that darkness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I know this may seem a strange question, but why didn't you, as a JNA officer, dare to go into the darkness at Velepromet? Can you just help me a little with that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly can. Throughout my time in the area, it was forbidden to move about at night - and this applied to us and to all other persons there - to prevent any confusion at check-points or with soldiers on duty, because they might simply be startled into causing a severe or serious incident. Therefore, the decision was to not move about at night, not in vehicles, not on foot, not outside, wherever you were, in a manner of speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could we please again ask for all the other microphones to remain off while the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if one looks at the Velepromet complex, were there areas that you could go that were reasonably illuminated but other areas where it was black and, as a matter of policy, you did not go; would that be a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The court-yard - the area between the buildings - was illuminated, but there was no illumination whatsoever behind those buildings or in the surrounding area. It was pitch black over there, and it was better not to go there so that no misfortune befell you, unless you had a reason to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us that you were there for approximately three hours, and I had prefaced the fact at the very start that you had only ever seen the attitude of Topola. Would it surprise you that Mr. Kijanovic reported that the TO threatened officers and people on the bus and that a gun was pulled out by Topola, Skorpion, and placed in Kijanovic's chest?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I do not know of that incident and I don't know where it was that it took place. As for people complaining, I wouldn't really say that any serious threats were uttered; but there were complaints being made but those people and they were coming over to speak to us, in the sense of telling us that we were there protecting those people who were there or who had been brought over. Whether they wanted to settle accounts with them or not is not something that I can say, but I didn't see anything like that happening. Had there been anything like that happening and we noticed, we certainly would have stopped it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you aware that we have had evidence from witnesses at the very early part of this trial who gave evidence about being held at Velepromet on the night of the 19th? Were you aware of that fact? Have you been told by anyone? We're not talking about JNA soldiers; we're talking about people who were actually held there. Now, were you aware of people giving such evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of such evidence being given. I know that there were people there, even later on. At that time, I found out that several people were being held in a room. I'm not sure about the size of that group. I do know that it was a small room. It's the same room in which I informed Bogdan Vujic about the presence of drunken TO men yelling and making a lot of noise. One of the group was this man nicknamed Topola. He must hail from the town of Topola, I suppose. Bogdan Vujic did go there. I wasn't with him, but I do know that he brought back a person from that room, someone who was injured with blood on his forehead. He brought him to that office and asked for Borisavljevic to come over and assist that person. This was the principal reason that the drunken TO men were complaining for, but this was certainly the only instance in which I actually saw blood at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We had a witness, a man called Josip Covic, and he was taken to Velepromet around 10.00 or 11.00 that night - the night you were there and at the time you were there - and he said the following, let's see if this assists whether you saw anything occurring. He was asked: "Were you placed inside or outside a hangar at this time; can you remember?" And he replied this -- in this way: "I remember it very well. I was in front of the hangar, as I was one of the people separated. We were lined up, and the local civilians passed next to our group pointing at certain people; and those people would then be taken behind the hangar some 50 metres away to Ciglana and they were killed there." Now, the reason I ask you, obviously it's Velepromet. It's a lining outside. But I want to ask you before we go any further, about "local civilians passing next to our group." Did you see local civilians assist in the identification of people, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the time we arrived at Velepromet to the time we left, there were no such groups passing by or through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I suggest a slight rephrasing of that reply, that you were aware of. You can only talk about what you are aware of, that's right, not whether it was occurring or not in other places; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can afford to be positive is some things for the simple reason that I spent all of the time outside within the perimeter, on the ground, as it were. As for any civilians arriving, particularly groups, this is definitely not something that I saw at the time, and I think I can be quite confident about this. One thing I'm perfectly confident about is that no killings occurred at a distance of a mere 50 metres from Velepromet. I am sure I would have heard that happening. Certainly not during the time that we were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that the record will be set straight because the answer appears to be the same thing as the question. If I look at the transcript -- line 4, page 50 is where the answer begins but since I'm interrupting Mr. Moore - but I didn't mean to interrupt him because of this - there was something that we had as a rule and this applied and obtained throughout the OTP case, please let's not name any names and especially not "witnesses" -- this is something that we adhered to throughout the OTP case whenever they had any objections to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with that same witness, the evidence that he gave. He said -- this is before the lining up: "Before that, there was a crime that took place. One of the civilians pointed out a young man. He said that his name was Kemo. I'm not absolutely certain, but it was a nickname of sorts, and he called two Chetniks to come. They came and they slit his throat in front of us." So I want to deal with that. I will go on, if I may, because there's a question and answer, in fairness to you. He then goes on to say - and it's at T3445, to assist the Court - "I told this person called Kemo that a civilian had come by. I recognised three civilians. There was one civilian who pointed out that particular young man - and this one I don't know - it was a lady who pointed him out. At this point, a TO man came along, came up to this young man, and he called over two Chetniks, two of Seselj's men who were wearing the full Chetnik attire. They had cockades on their fur caps. One of them wore the military kind and supported a long beard. There was a bottle containing some sort of drink sticking out of his pocket. He had knives on him, too, as well as an automatic rifle. They slit this young man's throat right in front of us. They gave him short shrift. The young man just lay there for 15 minutes." Now, I want to deal with three or four aspects of that evidence for you. Did you at any time see people referred to as Chetniks, to -- of Seselj's men who were wearing the full Chetnik attire? Did you ever see anyone at Velepromet, as far as you can remember, who were wearing the full Chetnik attire? If you can't remember, just say you can't remember.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I do know is that in the group that I informed Colonel Vujic about, there were drunken people wearing Chetnik uniforms and cockades. That is one thing that I know, but I heard nothing about anything like that happening even before our arrival. This is the first time I've ever heard that anyone's throat was slit at Velepromet. If indeed such a thing ever occurred, that was certainly before our arrival. But let me tell you one thing, I never heard of this happening at all, and the description would seem to fit Topola, to some extent; but then on the other hand, what do I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: They had cockades on their fur caps. Did you see people with fur caps and with cockades?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It also said: "He had knives on him," and I suspect knives were fairly common, "as well as an automatic rifle." Did you see people there at Velepromet who had automatic rifles, from memory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you let us know, just generally, how many people that you saw had perhaps automatic rifles? More than ten, or is it difficult to remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group that I saw, I don't think there were more than ten; secondly, I didn't really focus on what sort of weapons they were carrying. All were armed, and some even had knives tucked into their boots.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just -- I just want to deal with that same witness, some other evidence that he gave. The question was this: "When these people were taken away," I was talking about the people being taken away and shot - you have referred to the use of a silencer being used, because there was a suggestion of a silencer maybe being used. "When these people were being taken away, did you at any time hear gun-fire coming from the area where they were taken to? "A. Yes, I did hear gun-fire. This gun-fire continued throughout practically. There were lulls. And that would last two or three minutes and then the firing would start again. It was like this throughout, at least for as long as I was still at Velepromet." Now, would that be the sort of thing that you remember, hearing gun-fire? I'm not saying where it's directed. I'm just saying gun-fire throughout with lulls. Does that agree with your memory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the TO men and I saw our own men too, but nobody had silencers; and I heard no shots being fired anywhere near those facilities, and I am positive about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, I'll try and deal with this briefly. This same witness said about two Chetniks, they were some distance away, and they came up and started punching him. And he says the following: "At this point, to my great fortune, another JNA officer emerged from somewhere, called those two over, and ordered them to join him in an order to go and do a job." Now, I'm asking whether, in actual fact, you saw anyone being punched by Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, and I don't know who took them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This is another witness, it's 007 at T4028. This relates, if my memory serves me correctly, to the area, the court-yard area. I may be wrong, but I don't think I am. All right. And what he said is this: "During the transfer from Vupik," which was an area there, "to Velepromet, we were taken to a wall which is on the left side next to the Velepromet entrance. More people were being brought in from all directions. After a certain amount of time, not too long afterwards, I was summoned by a man called Miko Jankovic, a former waiter in Vukovar, from a group, and he told me to stand a little bit to the side. A young man stood next to me; I knew him from Ilok. He was a police officer in Vukovar at that time and he then gave his name. "Jankovic took him out from that group also and told him to stand next to me, next to that wall. After a certain amount of time, he cursed him, cursed his mother, and he then" -- or sorry, "then he hit him on the face with the barrel of his rifle. Blood started to show on his face, and then they took him off somewhere and I never saw him again." Now, this is the area that is in the court-yard area. Did you see anything like that occur, or might it have happened at some other time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this must have occurred before our arrival. Once we arrived, no persons were being brought into Velepromet from outside. If indeed this ever occurred, it must have been prior to our arrival, but I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's the second time you have said "if this ever occurred." Do you have an element of doubt that there were severe beatings in the Velepromet area, bearing in mind you'd been there afterwards for about three months?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't rule out the possibility. I am just telling you I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This same witness, 007 -- you were asked by Mr. Lukic about the atmosphere at Velepromet as you remember it. This was a question that was asked of the same witness that I've just mentioned. "Q. What was the atmosphere like in Velepromet at that time when you came in? "A. It's very difficult to describe it verbally. There was panic and fear in the air. Sounds of shooting could be heard from the moment I arrived throughout. This shooting - what should I call it? There was shooting all over the place. There was celebratory fire." That means celebrations. "People firing into the air and other people firing. I didn't know why they were firing. You could hear screams, women screaming for the most part: Bring back my this or my that, because they were taking people away and women were crying. It was a scene of utter chaos."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is being asked to comment and describe the situation, and the fact is we don't know when the witness was there and when he described the situation at Velepromet. I mean no time-line is indicated. Really, if he's being asked to comment on another person's evidence, we must know that this is in relation to a point in time when this particular witness was there. It wasn't my intention to explain the answer, but I think this is a very tall order for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. He seems to be well in control and command of the situation, nevertheless. Mr. Moore, are you able to indicate whether this scene occurred coincidently in time or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This was the 19th, the night of the 19th. It's at T4033. I hope that assists my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you then about this matter. He says it's difficult to describe verbally. Panic, was there panic? Could that be a fair word?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Panic, yes, there was panic even when we arrived, but things were more quiet in a way already. There was commotion. There was a confusion. There were territorials there, women, children, elderly, and those people had already been taken away to the hangars. Whatever happened must have happened prior to our arrival, but then again different perspectives are possible as well as different interpretations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was it a scene of utter chaos? That's the phrase he uses.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe at the outset there was utter chaos. Once we arrived, it was no longer chaos. As I say, people had already been separated off, those people who had been attacked by the TO men or whoever was there, but that was cleared up by the time we arrived; and the only people left were the TO men and ourselves until the time the buses arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to just move on a little bit quicker, if I may. This same witness described hearing firing outside the room, what is being called sometimes the room of death. He described firing just outside the door of that building and phrases like: "'He's getting away. He's getting away. Catch him quickly.' After a while a door opened, a young man was thrown or pushed into the building, both his legs were bleeding." Now, the time that he puts is around about 9.00 -- he says 9.00, half past 9.00, at the latest, that he was then told he would be executed. Did you hear in anybody trying to run off and shots occurring, or might that have occurred before you arrived also?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am certain it could only have happened before my arrival. We arrived later on; however, I never heard a single shot fired at Velepromet for as long as I was there. Therefore, this could only have been earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And this is the final witness I want to deal with, and I can deal with it fairly quickly. It's P032, it's T2965 and he says -- the question is asked and here is the reply: "Now, can we come back to Velepromet. You said, I believe, that you were taken to the room of death. Why was it called the room of death? "A. When we arrived at Velepromet, they took us straight there. They searched us, they beat us a little, and then they threw us into that room. "Q. How many people eventually were put into this room, roughly? "A. Between 50 and 60 persons. "Q. And roughly, how long did you stay in this room? "A. Three days." Now that is starting on the 19th. Obviously you are not there, 20th -- or perhaps 21st, but did you see people being searched and taken away, perhaps searched and being beaten? Did you see that occur?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any such thing, but there was constant work there because people were brought to Velepromet later on as well; but for somebody to be beaten, abused or killed, I didn't even hear about that from anyone because the situation had already been regulated, the relevant service and the police and there was some kind of reception desk there too. So at that reception desk, people knew who was who and where people were supposed to go. I really don't know about such cases, and I'm surprised that I don't know about that room.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said something about three days, but the interpreters could not hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, the question was: "What sounds or anything did you hear when people left the room? "A. There was a police officer there." Did you see a police officer at any time? "He was sitting inside a room when we came; he had a gashing wound across his face inflicted by a knife. He said he had been interrogated and his face was slashed by a knife." Do you know if there were interviews or interrogations at Velepromet, just generally? Do you know that? Do you know if there were interviews or interrogations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. We would have conducted the first interviews. We had other things to do. We dealt with Velepromet at the time, but when the situation was taken care of, we did not come to Velepromet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: They refer to gurgling and then nothing else, but can I just go back to your answer. Are you saying that you did do interviews or interrogation within that three-hour period? I'm sorry, it's my fault, not yours, for not understanding.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not have official interviews with anyone or interrogations. We were supervising the situation and we would exchange a few words with someone, but that was not an interview, an interrogation, or interviews as we called them, "informativni razgovor."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What was the purpose then of those brief interviews that you had?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part to see who was in this Velepromet, so I had these brief conversations with territorials as well so that there wouldn't be any incidents. We did our best not to have any incidents taking place, so the situation was quite calm. I'm really surprised by some things.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off when the witness speaks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you aware that local people or TOs, as I call them, were being used at various times in Vukovar to assess or to help in identifying who was who?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, yes. Later, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You see, we have a document - I think it is the 9th of October but I can't swear on it - where it refers to Borisavljevic being - and I'll try and use a neutral word - being at Velepromet to manage the selection procedure with local individuals assisting him in the identification of persons. Now, I can get the document if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be fair, if it's being brought up, to show the actual document, to read what it says because this is just an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I was trying to do it for speed, but I have got it here so it can help. It's the 10th of November, my apologies. So could we have Exhibit 835, please, for the B/C/S, and I have got the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Korica, you are going to have the benefit of electronic wizardry and have a document come up on your screen. Now do you see it there in front of you in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we just look at the top left-hand corner, it's the 10th of November, 1991. Now, you are most welcome to read the whole document if you want, but I, for my part, really only want to deal with the second paragraph. And it really should commence: "A centre for the admission of civilians and preservation of material goods." Have you got that particular paragraph? So it starts: "A centre for the admission of civilians and preservation of material goods." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll read it out so that nobody's disadvantaged. "A centre for the admission of civilians and preservation of material goods, Vukovar Group South has been set up within the offices of Velepromet, which is directly managed by Srecko Borisavljevic, First Class Captain, from the Guards Motorised Brigade security organ. Our first mechanism for finding extremists and possible disguised members of the MUP and the ZNG. The head of the centre, Ljubinko Stojanovic, businessman from Petrova Gora, who is otherwise a security organ source who was given detailed instruction in work on security matters when he came to Belgrade." This is the important part -- well, this is the part I want to concentrate on: "Six persons from various Vukovar local communes are continuously employed at the centre which facilitates the identification of local people. We have put in a request to have the number of staff at the centre increased and improve the security system and the control of movement in the liberated part of the town." Now, you're most welcome to read the rest of it if you wish, but what I'm trying to suggest to you is that we have a document where it says that it is Borisavljevic and that there are local people being used for identification purposes. Now, having seen that document, were you aware that at Velepromet, local people were being used to identify ZNG, MUP, and other parties?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, and it seems normal to me, natural to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you mind if I came back to the question and repeated it? Were you aware that that was what was happening, being normal or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was done later, whether civilians were used, but it wasn't necessary any longer to use civilians because there were employees of Velepromet who were local people, for the most part, from Territorial Defence. I know that this prominent man even had a little kiosk where he worked, and this was where the first identification of persons took place. Now, whether somebody helped him if he found something unclear and whether he sought assistance, I don't know, but I knew that he was there later, but now I see that he was there earlier on too. But that night you couldn't really see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you about the kiosk, what you mean by that. Where was that located?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That kiosk was in Velepromet later, when I stopped by Velepromet, later. Out there in front of that building - what do you call it? - the room of death, perhaps 10 metres in front of that, in the yard of Velepromet itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was the function of that kiosk or the people in the kiosk? What was its purpose?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one person was in that kiosk. That kiosk even gave people passes to move about in that zone. He issued passes. And he also checked the IDs of persons who came there and who he gave passes to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us about buses and people being placed on the buses that evening of the 19th. I'd like to just deal with that, if I may, for the moment. The buses -- when you went to Velepromet, you were expecting their arrival, is that correct, to assist in the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what we were waiting for, for them to arrive, so we didn't do much work except that we, in a way, were milling about amongst all those people and all that commotion. There were quite a few of us there. We could see quite a few things there. In all fairness, I didn't go into the hangars, but the rest I saw well. And -- anyway, later, these people were -- well, we were waiting for the buses. I don't know how long we were waiting, but the buses came soon and then what we organised was to have these people taken out of the hangars. They were brought from the hangars because the -- that's when the military came in, but until then, there was no military presence there. There were policemen there. There was a policeman at the entrance of, or rather, at the bus door too so nobody else could go in. And then when I got on to the bus, then I started writing all the these persons' names down, from the first to the last seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that Vujic had indicated that lists should be made of people going on to each bus, or am I wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're wrong because Vujic had no list until we handed the lists in. I handed in my list to Borisavljevic, and there were no markings on it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could all microphones please be switched off. We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question I've asked, it's probably because I have left the mike on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S, I heard a different interpretation of the question and the witness probably heard the same thing, so could the question please be repeated? Page 63, line 7. Perhaps the interpreters omitted something and that's why the witness gave the kind of answer he gave. So could it please be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just repeat the question. Am I right in saying that Vujic had indicated that lists should be made of people going on to each bus, or am I wrong about that? It's Vujic's suggestion for this.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a different question. That is what Vujic said. Vujic asked for these lists to be made. I made them and I handed them over to Borisavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask what is the purpose of a list in such circumstances, as far as you understand?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that if for no other reason, for the effectiveness of work, that when he would bring them to Sremska Mitrovica, he'd say: Here's the list, here's the men. So then the two could be compared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us about Topola coming at this time and being aggressive. That is correct, I think, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And without putting too fine a point on it, he's nothing more and was nothing more than a drunken lout that evening the way he was behaving; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He behaved terribly, a drunkard, a lout. I don't know how to categorise this person, a very unpleasant sort of person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is he a rather tall person as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's tall, with long hair, unshaven, with a long beard. He had a bandage around his hand. He had sort of injured himself in his drunkenness. Yes, he is tall, yes. He had an automatic rifle and a knife; I know he had that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I seem to remember you telling me that when he was at the bus, he had a -- what I will call a long-arm, perhaps others might call a rifle, where he was standing in a position holding the gun like this; is that correct? Is my recollection right or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He often held a rifle this way, lifted up this way, as if he would shoot up into the air. He wouldn't put it down. Now, what he wanted to know in that way and to whom, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you get the impression that he was behaving in an arrogant way in front of others?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his attitude was more arrogant than he, himself. Already by the morning, he would be different; he wouldn't be that way. But after a few brandies, again, he'd be the same. He did attack -- well, he followed Colonel Vujic around most of the time because Vujic took out this man who was given medical assistance; that's where they clashed. So the clash went on for a while, but not with the same kind of intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: One gets the impression that you consider Bogdan Vujic to be a rather fiery gentleman; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, but not very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When people were being put on the bus, can you remember approximately how many buses there were?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. At any rate, all the buses were full. All the seats had been taken and everybody was sitting down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You made a list, you had control of a bus; I think that is right, isn't it? And Vujic had control of the bus; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did Tomic have control of a bus? Kijanovic have control of a bus? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure, so I really don't want to make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember Tomic or Kijanovic ever giving you a list for you to hand on to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think your evidence was that when you went back to Negoslavci that evening, Tomic and Kijanovic were already there. I think that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you had travelled back by car?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came back in a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I know this may be a difficult question to answer, but would it be right to say that it was your impression that Tomic and Kijanovic had left Velepromet earlier than you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that they left before me. It's possible because for a while I really did not see them in Velepromet, so I don't know where they were. Had they left earlier or a lot earlier, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if one was trying to put it in sequence, it's at the end of your period there when you don't see Tomic and Kijanovic; that's why you can't say when they left?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if that could be an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore. And we will resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I just ask you about the arrival of the B-O-V, I think that's what it's called, I call it a BOV. Do you know what I'm talking about or ...

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's an armoured personnel carrier that arrived to accompany the evacuation, is that right, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. It's an APC or a BOV, if you like, that arrived with the buses to escort that convoy of buses as far as Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You were with Vujic most of the time at Velepromet, you have told us that; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You are aware that Vujic has said that a situation arose where the BOV vehicle was used by him to threaten a potential incident of violence about one of the rooms. Do you remember hearing about that from Mr. Lukic or indeed from anyone else?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I deal with this very quickly. What I'm going to suggest to you is this: You have no memory of seeing a BOV vehicle being used to support Vujic; that's right, I think, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I think I would have known, and that's not what I think it was used for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All I'm going to suggest to you is this: You're not saying it didn't happen. All you're saying is: If it happened, you don't remember seeing it. Would that be a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I could even go as far as to assert that. It would have been seen moving about the court-yard. I probably would have noticed with the headlights on and -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we'll agree to disagree on that. I thought, in fairness to you, I should put it to you. With regard to people being killed, you said that you did not see or know of anyone being killed at Velepromet; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you have also told us that within a group like this, often there is a transfer of information to assist others in their understanding at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Nobody told us about any killings at Velepromet, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I presume that you are aware that evidence was given in Belgrade by Kijanovic, where he stated that he had found bodies at Velepromet on the morning of the 20th. Were you aware of him saying that in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't follow the Belgrade trial, but I do happen to know that he said that. Bogdan Vujic told me about that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But as far as you are concerned, Kijanovic never mentioned it to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I did not have any particular conversations with Kijanovic at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think I understand where the error is, and it's my fault, actually. I've got it the wrong way around. So may I just clarify it if that is the objection. That in actual fact, Mr. Kijanovic, it's Mr. Kijanovic made a statement in relation to finding bodies at Velepromet, were you aware of that, not at Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's my objection. No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, if memory serves, even in the OTP statement - my learned friend probably has it in front of him - in his statement to the Belgrade court, Kijanovic said he had found dead bodies in the gardens behind Velepromet, which I think is very different, on the 20th. He said something about finding three dead bodies in the gardens behind Velepromet, and I think it would only be fair to put it that way to the witness since this circumstance is being put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In actual fact, I'm referring from the statement, and I will put it to the witness accurately. It's paragraph 40. "I discovered three to four bodies in the open space in the fields behind Velepromet on the 20th of November."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So were you aware that he was saying that subsequently?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogdan Vujic told me, he was the one, before evidence at the special court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were you aware in 2000 that Tomic had said at the special court that he knew that the day before, that's the 20th, there had been murders of prisoners at Velepromet and that he was present when 10 or 15 bodies were taken away from that area. Now, that is Tomic giving evidence on the 14th of March, 2000, at the military court in Belgrade. Were you aware of him saying that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember now, the evidence is being used from a witness that we talked a lot about, it was ruled out of this trial. If you remember what Bogdan Vujic testified and then Mr. Vasic objected, and Tomic is dead; and in that sense, there was this decision to not use his testimony. I think there is a ruling to that effect, a written one, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I actually don't have a recollection. I remember it was specifically with regard to the evidence as a whole, but I am putting a matter to this witness whether in actual fact he was aware that Tomic had made that statement; and secondly, whether this witness was aware of that conclusion or that statement by Tomic himself. If he says no, I move off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Neither Judge Thelin nor I recall now precisely what was said about [Realtime transcript read in error "by"] Tomic. It was quite a time ago I'm afraid. I think the course to be followed at the moment, Mr. Moore, is for you to put the question and get the answer. If there is any significance in the answer, it will be necessary for the Chamber to refresh its recollection and to see whether it should disallow that question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will put it again because it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You are aware -- at least you seem to be suggesting you are aware that Tomic had said to the Belgrade court that the day before, i.e., the 19th, there had been murders of prisoners at Velepromet and that he was present when 10 or 15 bodies were taken away from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I wonder if my learned friend Ms. Dokmanovic could just keep her voice down a little bit, please, with the utmost respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of that suggestion by Tomic or indeed that suggestion generally? Can you help me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Tomic's evidence, and what you said about Tomic, it's the first I hear about it. Not even Vujic ever told me anything about Tomic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So are you saying then that at no time when you were in Velepromet or Vukovar were you ever told by Kijanovic or Tomic about dead bodies. That is your final position on it; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th, I met Tomic and Kijanovic at 6.00 in the morning when I was off to the hospital. I didn't see them again that day, nor indeed did I hear from them; therefore, they couldn't possibly have told me anything about that, since I never spoke to them that day. Even later on when we left for Sid --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not get the final part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last part. You said even when you went to Sid, what happened after that, please? Can you just expand that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say even when we went to Sid. I said I didn't see them at all on that day because we went to Sid and they went to Negoslavci, and I never saw them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when this matter was over on the 20th, you did not see Tomic or Kijanovic again; would that be right? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The right thing to say would be I did not see them at all on that day, apart from the time I saw them at 6.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I ask you when the next time it was when you saw them, if you are able to tell us that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw them again at all, with the exception of Bogdan Vujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've told us that you went back to Negoslavci, so I want to move away from Velepromet and go back to Negoslavci in the early hours of the 20th. Can I deal with that topic, please. Is that all right? You know the area I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it's not all right. I wasn't in Negoslavci on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you not go back to -- did you not report back to the area where you had got your instructions from Mrksic and Sljivancanin? Mr. Lukic seems to be suggesting that the interpretation may be wrong. So shall I ask the question again if the interpretation is wrong?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you are asking me about the 20th and Negoslavci. I'm saying I was not in Negoslavci at all on the 20th. We left Ovcara and went straight to Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I'm talking about the very early hours of the morning of the 20th, 1.00 or 2.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a different matter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, that's the time I want to deal with. So you return back to Negoslavci, you agree? Yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We returned to Negoslavci that night, after we'd finished that job at Velepromet. That is all right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I failed to understand the first time around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Not a problem at all. Now, when you get back, you find Kijanovic and Tomic there. You then told us I think you went to have a bite to eat down below; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the cellar, yes, we had some canned food and then went back to the same place we were before. This only took a short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So is the situation that when you arrived back, you were asked whether you would like to have something to eat and you went down to the cellar to have something to eat then. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What was happening upstairs when you were eating?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, do I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You come back upstairs and I think you go into the same room, and you basically try and sleep in those chairs. Have I got the sequence right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you got it right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us move then, please, to 6.00 a.m. on the morning of the 20th, where you travel from Negoslavci to the hospital. I want to deal with that area of evidence. You've already told us that Sljivancanin had indicated to you what you were to do. You had taken lists or compiled lists at Velepromet. Did Sljivancanin tell you to compile lists at the hospital; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that, and I don't think he ever told me to compile any lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You get to the hospital, Sljivancanin is with I think a captain, is that right, another officer, Vujic, and yourself. Is my memory correct on that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you see Sljivancanin then standing up on something and addressing the crowd; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have heard evidence that on occasions, there were TO persons, paramilitary persons, who were at the hospital to help select or identify various individuals. Did you see that when you were there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was there, people were helping us. Were they TO men or not, I don't know, but I received a lot of assistance from someone who used to be a hospital employee before the war broke out. The same applied to the nurses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have heard the name of a hospital employee, his name was Bogdan Kuzmic, does that ring a bell? If you can't remember, just say if you're bad on names.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have such a good head for names, but I can't [Realtime transcript read in error "can"] say that particular one rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What were the people doing to help you in the selection process? Can you explain to the Court the tasks and functions.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even know that they had received any tasks at all, but they were helping us and had it not been for them, I would have had to request outside assistance, assistance from outside the hospital. For example, any staff who knew or recognised the people that I was taking outside. I don't know what their other tasks might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic has an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to interrupt, but I do have something about the transcript, it's page 75, line 2, this is not what the witness said. I won't be repeating that but I think his answer was entirely different from what was said in relation to Bogdan Kuzmic, so could we please have that question again and the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll see if I asked the right question. I take it it's the question at 74, 24, is that the question that -- very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I repeat the question, it's not your fault. We have heard the name of a hospital employee, his name was Bogdan Kuzmic, does that name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have such a good head for names, as I said, but I can't say that particular name rings a bell. I don't think I have ever heard that name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If it helps, Mr. Moore, I had noted that it doesn't ring a bell. Could I also mention that at page 70, line 24, I mentioned that neither Judge Thelin nor I could remember what was said and the transcript has the words "by Tomic"; what was intended was "about Tomic." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell just tell us then, please, exactly the procedure that what operating at the hospital for, what I will call, the selection, the triage. How were these people assisting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, if one of the persons selected by me to go were not medical staff, were not hospital employees, and had not left with those people that they were meant to leave with when they were allowed to go and head for Velepromet, if for example, I came across such a person and they defended themselves by saying they were hospital employees, that they were working at the hospital, or that they were previously employees, then I have to go to one of the staff to tell me whether this person in fact was a hospital employee or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The people who were selecting, let us take the -- what I will call the Sljivancanin vehicle. We have got Sljivancanin, we have got a captain, we have got yourself, we have got Vujic, and we have another. That's five, I think. And were there other officers who -- or indeed, soldiers from the JNA, as far as you could see, who were assisting in the triage? Because five doesn't seem a lot for a large number of people.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is there were doctors present there from the military hospital and from Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have heard evidence, obviously, from other individuals who were at the hospital, both from the Prosecution and from the Defence. With regard to JNA officers, what JNA officers did you see there at the hospital assisting in the triage?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the doctors from Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see tables or desks being used where individuals were being searched, for example, to check if they were carrying weapons or cold steel - I think is the phrase that was being used - before getting on the bus? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was done outside; it was done by the military police. It was done to all the persons we were bringing outside. They would go as far as the tables, they would take things out of their pockets, military police would check these things, and I would go back inside for the next round.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see anybody making a list at that time in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have heard evidence in what is called the Mitnica evacuation that there was quite a detailed list of 175 other ranks and I think 7 officers, and they were precise about the numbers. This was a group that went to Sremska Mitrovica. We have heard evidence today from you that you made accurate notes or lists of people getting on the buses. Can you explain why it was there was no list or lists being compiled in relation to the people who were going on to that bus that eventually ended up in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Being absolutely honest about it - which I'm sure you are, and I'm not suggesting in any way you are not - isn't it right you would have expected a list to be compiled?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but I don't think that I expected it to be compiled in the hospital, because it would not have been a single list. I could have compiled a list in the hospital only of the persons that I took out, and I don't even know whether it's them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But isn't it right that the people in the triage, from what you have told us, the hospital people were not going to go on the buses, the women were not going to go on the buses, but the men who could walk were going to go on the buses. That was the classification that you understood; isn't that right? Do you remember your evidence at the start?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said, that's for sure, that that was the classification that existed, because I didn't know who would be doing the transporting and how and from where. I just knew that they were supposed to go to Sremska Mitrovica. As for the boarding of vehicles and so on, I don't know about that. Women were on one side and men on the other. When the women got out, I don't know. I just took the men out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But as far as you were aware, if the person was a hospital employee or was linked to the hospital and was a man, he almost certainly was not going to go on the bus, but other men were; isn't that right? I see you nodding.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if that is the case, those men were being searched by the military police to check about cold steel; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And also, if there was to be a list compiled, it could have been compiled at the time when they were distributing or leaving their cold steel on the table; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you just to reflect upon that? Is that not the time when you would compile a list where the people who were going on to the bus were being searched before they went? Isn't that the time you would make a list?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could be that moment, but it can also be the moment of the boarding of the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could Your Honour forgive me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have heard evidence that the security -- and seen evidence that the security organ had names of individuals who, perhaps, would be considered to be MUP, HDZ, or persons who had committed atrocities. We have heard and seen this evidence. Were you aware of the existence of a list of people who were known to be involved in, perhaps, criminal acts against Serbs and other people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of any such list, that's for sure. And if that list did exist, then it's possible that Mr. Sljivancanin had it or Vujic, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vujic went to Velepromet, isn't that right, after the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And Mr. Sljivancanin - as you indicated to us at the very outset - had indicated that things had to be done and completed before the ICRC arrived; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it was Mr. Sljivancanin who was indicating to Colonel Vujic what was required of you all; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I move on, please, to Velepromet, what I will call the Velepromet meeting evidence. I suspect you know what I'm talking about. You get there, and is it right that you find Borisavljevic there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Borisavljevic when he got out of the office where they had the meeting, Vujic, Kijanovic, and I don't know who else was there too, because I was not at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with the brief-case incident. Now, I think it is right to say that Borisavljevic brought the brief-case to the office where I think you and Vujic were located; is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The brief-case contained, did it not, a large number of wallets; that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a large number. I think about three wallets and two envelopes, something like that. I'm not sure now how many there were. I may make a mistake, say, of one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well I won't hold that against you. Can I just deal with the wallets themselves. Did the wallets have items inside them or were they completely empty?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wallets were full.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. And when we talk about full, some wallets are fuller than others. Was there money in the wallets sometimes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In every one of the wallets, there was money, there were Deutschemark, there were dollars, there were dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well I was going to suggest to you about the dollars and Deutschemarks. Was there also documents in the wallet that tended to suggest the identification of the person?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in all wallets, there were personal IDs and also other documents in those wallets, and I wrote down all the particulars from those documents as well as all the bank notes, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And am I right in my recollection when you gave your evidence, and indeed when you spoke to me, that you had been told by Borisavljevic that you said in evidence here his man, a policeman, but I'd suggest - and it is only my memory, and I can check it - that when you were speaking to me upstairs, you referred to "his men" had found them nearby. Now, can I just try and clarify this. I'm not trying to catch you out any way at all. Is it a case that Borisavljevic told you either that his man or his men had found the brief-case; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that his man had found that brief-case, handed it over to him, and that he didn't have time to handle that; so he asked us to look into this and to have it handed over to the security administration because we would be going to Belgrade before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And again, is it right to say that Borisavljevic indicated that the location of the finding of the wallet, the brief-case and wallets, was in what I will call the general Velepromet area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the general area. He said he found it behind the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, it's my fault for the way I put it, but it's in the general hangar area of Velepromet. My fault. Now --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- I'm right in saying, I believe, that in your evidence here, you thought - I will use the English phrase - you were being set-up by the paramilitaries or the TO. "Set-up" means "framed" in American language; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first that's what I thought. I mean, that they needed that in view of the fact that they were angry at us and they were objecting, that they were trying to discredit us in that way, and - how should I put this? - to put us down in front of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But would I be right in saying that that was your original view -- but bearing in mind what had happened the night before with Topola and the arrogance, would it be right to say that you put two and two together and thought perhaps there was more to this than met the eye? Do you understand the phrase? I can rephrase it if it's a difficulty.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing that came to mind was what I told you, well, this framing; then secondly, I was aware, during the course of my previous work before I ever came to Vukovar, that at some check-points - when entering the village, when leaving the village - some people were brought in and some policemen or soldiers took away documents from people, and we corrected that. We went around explaining this to these people who were setting up these check-points that you are not supposed to take away peoples' documents. So I did not rule out that possibility, that some soldier had made a mistake and had taken away the documents of the people who had come to Velepromet, and that was the first thing that came to my mind. But what you said, this third option, is something that crossed my mind too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why did you think the third option was a possibility?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think of it very much, but everything is possible, anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to ask about Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask if we could go into chambers -- in closed session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us about Arkan and Vujic or Vujic, I think, suggesting that the military police should bring Arkan to he, Vujic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the second order to the policemen, because Arkan did not want to come when first summoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But when Arkan came, came into the office with Vujic there, You are a crazy colonel, you are just an ordinary fool, how did Vujic react to that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: His reaction was very strong. He was all worked up. He didn't know what to do. And then he said, Did you come to kill here too? That's when he said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it was then that you tried to pacify the situation saying, If you kill one here, five -- Tudjman will kill five. So you, basically, were trying to suggest to Arkan to behave and not to behave irresponsibly, and not to kill anybody; that's what you were trying to do, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely because of killings, not only because of killings, I said if he expels or kills one person, or has the population of a village moved out, that Tudjman would move out the population of five of those villages of mine in Croatia where I was born. But in order to pacify the situation between the two of them, that was my intention. The two of them were tense. Arkan didn't seem that tense as Vujic. He got Vujic so upset, so I didn't want to have an incident that would be worse there, and that is why I tried to calm things down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And Arkan, as far as you are aware, had attended the government meeting or was to attend the government meeting at that time; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan attended the government meeting, and he invited Vujic to come to the government meeting and Vujic said: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And wouldn't it be right to say that Vujic, when he went to the government meeting, as far as you are aware, Vujic was trying to take a position to protect individuals and not release them away from JNA custody?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You weren't at the government meeting, this I know, and we're not suggesting that you were; but Vujic came back and told you his account. We also have heard evidence here. As far as you were aware from Vujic, Vujic's position was that he was standing against people like Arkan and not letting them take control of these prisoners, that he was trying to retain the custody of those prisoners, custody remaining with the JNA. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is it also right to say the reason that he was doing that was because he was afraid that something would happen to those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the objection is self-evident. I thought you be would be able to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's so late in the day, I doubt I will be able to respond at all. May I use Mr. Weiner's technique and say: I withdraw the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm glad Boston is teaching Belfast something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to move on to a different topic, and can I try and piggyback Mr. Korica's fatigue and ask if this would be an appropriate moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Moore, you feel it would be more profitable if we spent a shorter time tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will. I will definitely try to be shorter tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I'm interested in. Could I know a bit more specifically what the time would be? Now I see that Mr. Moore has the lead in terms of time. He's spent more time with this witness than I did, and I need to know so that I could tell you tomorrow about next week, what you asked me about. So our next witness is ready. But I still need to know, so I believe that it would be helpful to everyone, but our team in particular, if we were to stick to the original schedule for next week. So could we please know how long Mr. Moore is going to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will finish within the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Are you in a position, Mr. Lukic, to forecast how you will be in completing, whether we need to sit longer hours on the days that are available next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tell you tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must know tomorrow. We will adjourn now. We will resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
